questions.stem: How can setting contribute to the representation of people in a text?
options: Details of place build mood and suggest things about the lives lived there
Setting only establishes where and when events happen, affecting nothing else
A setting must be a real, named location or readers can conclude nothing
Descriptions of place always stand for the main character's state of mind
questions.explanation: Place and people are represented together: heat, dust, locked gates or crowded flats all carry implications about the conditions and values of the characters living there. The claim that setting merely tells us where and when is the common trap — it describes one function of setting while denying the meaning-making the rest of the description depends on. Test yourself by asking what a place detail implies about the people, not just where it puts them.

questions.stem: Why does knowing a text's historical and social context help you analyse how it represents people?
options: Context is irrelevant, since a representation is judged on the words alone
Texts from earlier periods cannot represent people recognisably to readers today
Context explains which attitudes and assumptions shaped the author's choices
Older texts represent people more accurately, being closer to the events
questions.explanation: Representations are made within a time and place, so understanding the beliefs circulating when a text was written clarifies why certain groups are shown as they are and what has been left unsaid. The claim that context is irrelevant sounds rigorous, but the curriculum task is precisely to read representations against their historical, cultural and social contexts. The cue is 'why this, then?' — a choice that seems odd now often makes sense against the attitudes of its era.

questions.stem: A novel set in a mining town is narrated in first person by a seventeen-year-old who is desperate to leave. What is the most accurate statement about the town's representation?
options: The representation is unaffected by the narrator, because the facts of the setting stay the same
Her narration presents the range of views the town's residents hold about living there
The town is filtered through her frustration, so it is likely to appear narrow and stifling to readers
First-person narration removes bias, since the narrator reports only what she directly observes
questions.explanation: A first-person narrator's attitudes act like a filter: the details she notices and the words she chooses shape the version of the town readers receive. The 'removes bias' option is the seductive one, because direct observation feels trustworthy, but observing is selective — what she chooses to see is exactly where the bias lives. Ask who is telling it and what they want, and you will predict the slant of the representation.

questions.stem: Read this opening: 'The town lay flat under a bleached sky, its shopfronts boarded, the war memorial still the tallest thing for forty kilometres.' How is the place represented?
options: As a thriving regional centre, since a war memorial signals civic pride and continuing investment
As a threatening place, since 'bleached' and 'boarded' warn readers that violence is coming
As an unknowable place, since the narrator supplies no concrete details about its size or condition
As a diminished community, with the memorial suggesting its past now overshadows its present
questions.explanation: 'Bleached', 'flat' and 'boarded' drain colour and activity from the town, while the memorial being the tallest structure implies nothing built since has mattered as much. The 'thriving regional centre' option reads the memorial as a positive symbol in isolation, ignoring the words around it — meaning comes from the whole pattern of detail. When analysing, group the image words together and ask what impression they build as a set.

questions.stem: In many literary works by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors, how is Country commonly represented?
options: Only in the distant past, since such works do not use contemporary Australian settings
As a living presence tied to family, story and responsibility, with people belonging to it
As empty wilderness waiting to be explored and made productive by newcomers
In a single shared style, since all First Nations authors write about the same one region
questions.explanation: Writing by First Nations authors frequently represents Country as animate and relational — connected to kin, story and obligations of care — rather than as property or scenery. The 'empty wilderness' option describes the colonial representation these works often challenge, so attributing it here reverses the relationship. Note also that First Nations writing spans many distinct nations, genres and time settings, including present-day city life.

questions.stem: A narrator describes a neighbour as 'one of those people who never mow, never wave, never bother'. What is the strongest analytical point about this representation?
options: The listing of three failings gives readers reliable evidence that the neighbour is antisocial
The sentence is purely descriptive, so it characterises the neighbour without positioning readers at all
The neighbour cannot be analysed as a character, because the passage reports no speech or action
The repeated 'never' and the dismissive grouping reveal the narrator's judgement as much as the neighbour
questions.explanation: The triple 'never' and the phrase 'one of those people' turn an individual into a type, so the language exposes the narrator's habit of judging while it describes the neighbour. The option treating the three failings as reliable evidence is the trap: readers only have the narrator's framing, not the neighbour's side of it. The cue is generalising language such as 'one of those' — it usually reveals more about the speaker than the subject.

questions.stem: Your first impression of a poem is that it is bleak, but on rereading you notice repeated images of seeds and rain. What is the most useful next step in developing your response?
options: Discard the bleak reading, since the later reading is based on closer attention to imagery
Record both readings separately and leave it to the reader to decide which is more convincing
Keep the bleak reading, because a first impression captures the poem's immediate effect most honestly
Explain how the seed and rain images sit alongside the bleakness, and what tension that creates
questions.explanation: Developing a response means holding both observations together and analysing the tension, since a poem can be bleak and still carry images of renewal. Discarding the bleak reading is the strongest distractor, but a later impression does not cancel an earlier one — the bleakness was produced by real features of the poem too. The productive move is almost always 'both, and how do they interact', not 'either, or'.

questions.stem: In a small-group discussion, a classmate argues that a short story's ending is hopeful, while you had read it as defeated. What is the most productive way to use this disagreement?
options: Ask which details led to the hopeful reading and test them against the details behind yours
Take a vote so the group can settle on the single reading it will present to the class
Change your reading, since a shared interpretation is more reliable than an individual one
Keep your reading unchanged, because a personal response cannot be judged by other readers
questions.explanation: Discussion develops a response by exposing the evidence behind each reading, which lets you test, refine or extend your own interpretation. Refusing to move because a personal response 'cannot be judged' is a common misconception: personal responses are still accountable to the text, even though more than one defensible reading can exist. The cue is evidence — ask what in the text produced the other reading before deciding whether it changes yours.

questions.stem: What most changes a reader's impression of a character on a second reading?
options: Knowing the ending, which makes early hints in behaviour visible
Reading more slowly, which increases how much plot is remembered
Learning the author's biography, which reveals the intended meaning
Discussing it, which corrects misreadings made the first time
questions.explanation: Rereading with knowledge of the outcome lets you register foreshadowing and small inconsistencies that passed unnoticed the first time, so the character can look quite different. Learning the author's biography sounds plausible but the claim is false: biography may add context, it does not reveal a fixed intended meaning that settles the character. The reliable trigger for a shifted impression is new attention to detail in the text itself.

questions.stem: A student's response reads: 'I found the ending frustrating.' Which addition would most improve it as a developed personal response?
options: Adding that many other readers in the class were also frustrated by the ending
Softening it to 'some readers may find the ending frustrating' to sound less personal
Replacing 'frustrating' with a precise summary of the events of the final chapter
Naming what the ending withheld and why that withholding produced frustration
questions.explanation: A developed response links the reaction to the specific textual choice that caused it, so 'frustrating' becomes an argument rather than a verdict. Softening the wording to sound less personal is a common instinct but it weakens the response: hedging removes the reader without adding evidence. Ask 'because of what, exactly?' — the answer to that question is the part worth writing.

questions.stem: Two students reread the same novel and end up with different final impressions of the protagonist, each quoting closely from the text. What does this best show?
options: Personal responses are simply matters of taste and cannot be compared for strength
The novel is poorly constructed, since a clear text would produce agreement among readers
A text can support more than one defensible reading, so responses must be argued from evidence
One student must have overlooked evidence, since a single reading is ultimately correct
questions.explanation: Literary texts are open enough that different readers can build different defensible interpretations, which is why the quality of a response rests on the reasoning and evidence supporting it. The claim that one student must have overlooked evidence is the most tempting distractor, but it assumes a single correct reading, which is not how interpretation of literature works. Multiple defensible readings still do not mean all readings are equal — an unsupported reading remains weak.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a personal response to a text from a plot summary?
options: It records the reader's first reaction and avoids changing it afterwards
It explains the reader's reaction and grounds it in details of the writing
It retells the main events in order so an unfamiliar reader can follow
It states an opinion only, since evidence would make it less personal
questions.explanation: A personal response reports what a text made you think or feel and then points to the language, characters or structure that produced that effect, so the reaction becomes arguable rather than just asserted. The tempting option is the one saying evidence would make the response 'no longer personal' — in fact quoting the text is what turns a private reaction into a response another reader can follow and test. The cue: a personal response always answers 'what in the text did that to me?'

questions.stem: On a first reading, a student finds a novel's narrator warm and reliable. Rereading, they notice the narrator's claims are repeatedly contradicted by what other characters say in dialogue. What is the best account of what has happened?
options: The narrator's warmth is now irrelevant, since only the second impression counts as a valid reading
Evidence noticed on the second reading has revised the student's impression of the narrator's reliability
The student's first impression was simply a misreading and should be left out of any written response
The contradictions show the writer has made an error in constructing the narrator's account
questions.explanation: Subsequent impressions form when a reader notices textual detail they missed the first time, and here the gap between the narrator's claims and others' dialogue is evidence of unreliability. The most tempting distractor calls the first impression a misreading to be discarded, but the narrator's initial warmth is deliberately created by the writer and explaining it is part of the analysis. The cue: a shift in impression is usually the text working on you in stages, not you failing at reading.

questions.stem: A film shows a protester filmed from below in slow motion, lit from behind, while the police line is filmed from a distance in flat grey light. How do these visual choices work on the audience?
options: Camera angle, pace and lighting make the protester appear heroic and the police impersonal
The scene is factual footage, so the visual choices cannot affect a viewer's sympathies
The choices only affect how attractive the scene looks, not how viewers judge the people in it
The low angle makes the protester appear weaker, so viewers are positioned to pity them
questions.explanation: Low angles grant a subject stature, slow motion and backlighting lend significance, and distant flat lighting withholds individuality — together these choices push viewers towards approving of the protester. The option saying a low angle makes the subject look weaker reverses the conventional effect: it is high angles looking down that tend to diminish a subject. Remember the direction: camera below means the subject looms larger.

questions.stem: Which of these is a language feature most directly used to shape a reader's moral judgement of a character?
options: Emotive vocabulary describing the character's actions and motives
The number of chapters in which the character appears
The tense used consistently throughout the narrative
The alphabetical ordering of names in a list of characters
questions.explanation: Emotive vocabulary attaches feeling to a character's behaviour, so it directly guides approval or disapproval. Chapter count is tempting because prominence does matter to a reader's impression, but simply counting appearances tells you nothing about whether the character is presented as admirable or contemptible. Look for words that carry judgement, not for structural statistics.

questions.stem: In a novel, a wealthy family's dinner is described in long, flowing sentences full of rich detail, while the scenes in the servants' kitchen are told in short, blunt sentences. What does this contrast in sentence structure most likely do?
options: It shows the author found the kitchen scenes less interesting to write about
It proves the novel approves of the wealthy family, since their scenes are given more words
It has no effect on meaning, because sentence length is a matter of the author's personal style
It reinforces the gap between the two worlds and directs attention to the inequality between them
questions.explanation: Syntax carries meaning: expansive sentences suggest ease and abundance, clipped ones suggest constraint and labour, so the contrast makes the social divide felt as well as described. The option that more words equals approval is tempting but confuses quantity with endorsement — lavish description can just as easily expose excess as celebrate it. Ask what the rhythm makes you feel about each world before deciding which side the text favours.

questions.stem: A charity poster shows a young girl looking straight out at the viewer, filling most of the frame, lit warmly, with a blurred crowd behind her. How do these choices work on the audience?
options: The blurred background proves the crowd is unimportant to the charity, so the viewer will judge the organisation as dishonest
The warm lighting removes any moral appeal, leaving the viewer to respond only to the poster's factual information
The girl filling the frame shows the photographer had no room to work, so the viewer notices technique rather than message
The direct gaze and warm close framing create a personal demand for sympathy, making the viewer weigh the crowd's needs through her
questions.explanation: A demand gaze plus a close, warmly lit shot builds an individual relationship with the viewer, and the blurred crowd behind makes her stand in for many — an ethical appeal built entirely from visual choices. The option about the blurred background 'proving' the crowd is unimportant misreads a compositional choice as a statement of the charity's values; blurring directs attention rather than dismissing what is blurred. Ask what each visual choice invites you to feel, not what it accidentally reveals.

questions.stem: When analysing how a writer's word choice shapes judgement of a character, what does the term "connotation" refer to?
options: A comparison between two unlike things made using 'like' or 'as'
The associations and feelings a word carries in addition to its literal meaning
The dictionary meaning of a word, fixed and unaffected by its context
The repetition of the same consonant sound at the start of nearby words
questions.explanation: Connotation is the emotional and cultural baggage of a word — 'crowd', 'mob' and 'gathering' can describe the same people while inviting very different judgements. The option about the fixed dictionary meaning describes denotation, which is the term connotation is usually contrasted with. Remember: denotation is what a word points at, connotation is how it makes you feel about it.

questions.stem: A novel introduces a guest at a dinner party like this: 'He circled the table, sniffing at each plate, then hunched his shoulders over the last of the bread.' What is the most accurate analysis of this description?
options: The onomatopoeia in 'sniffing' works to make the scene sound realistic rather than to shape judgement
The animal imagery invites the reader to judge him as greedy and predatory, discouraging sympathy
The description confirms he is literally starving, so the reader is required to approve of his actions
It is neutral descriptive detail that establishes the setting without affecting judgement of him
questions.explanation: Verbs borrowed from animal behaviour — circled, sniffing, hunched — build a figurative pattern that dehumanises the character and steers the reader towards distaste before he has spoken. The option about him literally starving reads figurative language as factual reporting, and even a starving character would still be shaped by the writer's choice of animal verbs. The cue is to ask what kind of creature the verbs belong to, not just what the sentence reports.

questions.stem: A poem about grief begins by calling the speaker's loss 'a house I still live in', then goes on for four stanzas describing its cold rooms, locked doors and unlit hallways. Which device is being used?
options: An allegory, since the poem tells a story that stands for a political event
Metonymy, since the house is named instead of something closely associated with it
Hyperbole, since the poem exaggerates the speaker's feelings for effect
An extended metaphor, since one comparison is developed in detail across the poem
questions.explanation: An extended metaphor takes a single comparison and sustains it, adding related details (rooms, doors, hallways) so that the image keeps doing work across a whole text. Calling it allegory is the tempting error, but allegory needs a sustained narrative in which characters and events correspond to another set of ideas or historical events, not just one image developed over four stanzas. Cue: one image elaborated = extended metaphor; a whole story with a parallel meaning = allegory.

questions.stem: In a short story, a character's cracked pocket watch is mentioned when she leaves home, again when she refuses a job, and finally when she returns to her father's grave. The best analysis of the watch is that it functions as:
options: An allegory, because the story as a whole retells the history of her family's town
A symbol, whose repeated placement at turning points builds meaning about time and loss
An intertextual reference, because broken clocks appear in many other well-known stories
Metonymy, because the watch is used in place of the word for her father
questions.explanation: Symbolism depends on placement and repetition: an ordinary object is returned to at significant moments until it carries meaning beyond itself. The intertextual option is tempting because motifs do travel between texts, but an intertextual reference requires the story to point deliberately at a specific other text, not merely use a common image. Cue: ask whether the meaning is built inside this text (symbol) or borrowed from a named outside text (intertextuality).

questions.stem: A news report states: 'Wall Street reacted badly, while Canberra stayed silent.' Which analysis of this language is accurate?
options: Both are symbolism: the two places represent abstract ideas of greed and duty
Both are extended metaphor: one comparison is developed across the whole sentence
Both are metonymy: place names stand in for the financial sector and the federal government
Both are personification: places are given the human abilities to react and stay silent
questions.explanation: Metonymy names something by a closely associated term, so 'Wall Street' does duty for financial markets and 'Canberra' for the federal government. The personification option is tempting because the verbs 'reacted' and 'stayed silent' sound human, but the substitution itself is what is doing the work — the places already denote groups of people who genuinely can react. Cue: check whether a name has been swapped for an associated institution before reaching for personification.

questions.stem: An essay claims: 'The rising sea in the novel is a symbol of colonisation.' Which addition would most strengthen this as an analysis of the device's effect?
options: Stating that many readers would interpret the sea differently depending on their background
Tracing where the sea image appears and showing what the pattern makes readers feel or realise
Adding that symbolism is a device in which an object represents something beyond itself
Naming two other novels published in the same decade that also feature rising seas
questions.explanation: Analysing a device means showing how it works on the reader — where it is placed, how it builds, and what effect that patterning creates — not simply asserting a meaning. Defining symbolism is the tempting choice because it sounds knowledgeable, but a general definition adds nothing about this text's effect. Cue: strong analysis moves from 'what it means' to 'how the text makes it mean that, and what it does to me as a reader'.

questions.stem: A story about two feuding families is titled 'Star-Crossed', and its lovers first talk across a balcony. Which device?
options: Extended metaphor, comparing the feud to one image across the story
Intertextual reference, drawing on an earlier text to shape expectations
Metonymy, replacing the families' names with a closely linked object
Allegory, in which every character stands for a political idea
questions.explanation: The title phrase and the balcony scene both point the reader towards Romeo and Juliet, so meaning is created by borrowing from a text outside this one — that is intertextuality. The allegory option is wrong because nothing here sets up a consistent second layer of political meaning for each character; a suburban feud read alongside Shakespeare is a reference, not a coded parallel. The cue for intertextuality is a recognisable borrowed name, title, plot or image that carries associations from another text.

questions.stem: In poetry, what is enjambment?
options: A line of poetry that runs on into the next line without a pause in grammar or punctuation
A strong pause created by punctuation at the end of a line, closing off the sense
The repetition of a whole line or phrase at the start of several consecutive stanzas
A rhyme that occurs within a single line rather than at the ends of two lines
questions.explanation: Enjambment is the running-on of a sentence or phrase past the line break, which can create momentum, breathlessness or a surprise as the meaning completes. The description of a strong pause at the end of a line is the tempting opposite — that is an end-stopped line. Remember that enjambment 'strides over' the break, while end-stopping halts at it.

questions.stem: Which is a choice about TEXT STRUCTURE rather than a language feature?
options: Describing grief as a stone lodged permanently beneath her ribs
Repeating a hard 'k' sound to make the description feel clipped
Using slang and contractions to signal a narrator's age and background
Telling events out of order, opening at the funeral and moving back
questions.explanation: Text structure refers to how a whole text is organised and sequenced — chapter order, flashbacks, framing narratives, cyclical endings. Rearranging the chronology is a structural choice. The metaphor about grief as a stone is tempting because it is a striking crafted effect, but working at the level of an image makes it a literary device, not the shape of the text. Ask yourself whether the choice is about the arrangement of the whole or the texture of a phrase.

questions.stem: Read this line: 'The sea slid soft across the shingle, seeping past the stones and settling in the sand.' Which analysis of its sound is accurate?
options: The repeated vowel sounds create assonance, giving the line a chiming, almost rhyming quality
The clustered plosive consonants give the line an abrupt, clipped pace that resists being read slowly
The internal rhyme between the stressed words locks the line into a regular marching rhythm
The repeated 's' sounds create a soft, hushing sound texture that echoes the movement being described
questions.explanation: Sibilance is the repetition of 's' and related hissing sounds, and here it slows the reading voice and produces a soft whispering effect that imitates water over stones. The assonance option is the most tempting distractor, but assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds and the pattern in this line is clearly consonantal. Check which letters actually repeat before naming the device.

questions.stem: A novel opens with a girl standing at a gate watching a bushfire on the horizon, and closes twenty years later with the same woman at the same gate watching rain. What aesthetic effect does this structural choice most likely create?
options: A sense of realism, because real memories always return people to the exact places they began
A sense of circularity that invites readers to measure change by holding the two moments against each other
A sense of confusion, since repeating an image at the end suggests the narrative has failed to progress
A sense of suspense, because repeating an opening scene traditionally signals an unresolved cliffhanger
questions.explanation: A cyclical structure frames the narrative so that the closing image rhymes with the opening one, and the differences between them (fire against rain) carry the meaning of everything that happened in between. The 'confusion' option misreads repetition as a fault: deliberate framing is a recognised structural technique, not a sign of a stalled plot. Look for what has changed inside a repeated frame — that contrast is where the effect lives.

questions.stem: A poem about a drought repeats the phrase 'and still no rain' at the beginning of each of its five stanzas. What is the strongest analysis of this device?
options: The anaphora builds an insistent, chant-like rhythm that makes the waiting feel drawn out and inescapable
The repetition functions as a rhyme scheme, binding the stanzas together into a fixed traditional form
The repeated phrase is onomatopoeic, since its sound imitates the noise of dry wind across paddocks
The repetition is a metaphor, because it compares the drought to a religious chant heard in a church
questions.explanation: Repetition at the start of successive lines or stanzas is anaphora, and its aesthetic effect here is rhythmic accumulation: each return of the phrase enacts the monotony and endurance of waiting. The rhyme-scheme option is tempting because repetition does bind stanzas, but a rhyme scheme is a pattern of matching end sounds, not a repeated opening phrase. If the same words return in the same position, name it repetition or anaphora, not rhyme.

questions.stem: Which sentence goes beyond identifying a device to analysing the aesthetic quality it creates?
options: The clipped, verbless fragments in the chase scene fracture the prose, so the reading itself feels breathless
The writer uses several short sentence fragments without verbs during the chase scene in chapter six
The chase scene is exciting to read and shows that the author is skilled at writing fast-paced action
Sentence fragments are a language feature in which a group of words is punctuated as a full sentence
questions.explanation: Analysis of aesthetic quality names the technique and then explains the effect it produces on the reader's experience of the text. Merely stating that the writer uses fragments in a chapter is identification, and the 'exciting to read' option is an unsupported evaluation that never links the effect to a specific choice. The test is whether the sentence connects a named feature to a described effect in the same breath.

questions.stem: A novel is narrated by a man whose name is withheld until the final page, where another character finally says it aloud. What is the most defensible analysis of this structural choice?
options: Withholding the name makes the text non-fiction in style, because factual reports avoid naming their sources
Withholding the name removes the narrator's personality, so readers cannot form any impression of him at all
Withholding the name keeps the narrator unplaced for the reader, so the delayed naming lands as a moment of recognition
Withholding the name proves the narrator is lying to the reader, since honest narrators always identify themselves early
questions.explanation: Delaying information is a structural device: the absence of a name sustains a slight distance or anonymity, and the eventual naming gives the ending weight because a withheld detail arrives at the point of greatest pressure. The claim that withholding proves dishonesty is tempting because unnamed narrators often feel evasive, but there is no rule linking anonymity to unreliability. Ask what the delay does to the reader's experience rather than assuming a fixed meaning for the technique.

questions.stem: A short story is told in reverse chronological order: it opens with one friend's funeral and ends with the two friends meeting for the first time as children. Which analysis best explains the aesthetic quality this structure creates?
options: Reversing the order removes suspense completely, so the story must depend only on vivid imagery to hold a reader's interest
Reversing the order makes the narration unreliable, since a narrator who reports events out of sequence cannot be trusted on detail
Reversing the order is a language feature working at sentence level, so its effect is best analysed through the writer's word choice
Placing the death first casts every earlier scene in dramatic irony, so the hopeful first meeting reads as poignant rather than simply happy
questions.explanation: Aesthetic quality comes from the effect an ordering choice has on the reader: because we already know the friendship ends in death, later-read (earlier-happening) scenes carry an ache the characters cannot feel, which is dramatic irony and produces poignancy. The claim that reversal removes suspense completely is tempting, because chronological suspense about the outcome does disappear, but the story simply shifts to a different tension — how and why the ending came about — so 'completely' and 'only imagery' make it false. Reversal is also a text-structure choice about the whole text, not a sentence-level language feature, and out-of-order telling is not evidence of an unreliable narrator. Cue: ask what the ordering makes the reader know and feel, not just what it takes away.

questions.stem: A Year 9 student is writing a two-minute spoken monologue to persuade Year 5 students at assembly to join the school garden club. Which set of choices best matches this purpose and audience?
options: Short, direct sentences, a repeated call to action and concrete images of the food they would grow
Detailed statistics on soil chemistry, a formal thesis statement and a list of cited sources
An ambiguous ending that leaves listeners unsure what the speaker actually wants them to do
Abstract metaphors sustained over several long paragraphs and left for listeners to unpack
questions.explanation: Purpose and audience together drive the choices: a persuasive spoken text for younger listeners needs immediate comprehension, memorable repetition and concrete detail they can picture. The abstract metaphors option is tempting because sustained imagery is a genuine literary technique, but held over long paragraphs and unexplained it defeats a two-minute spoken persuasion aimed at Year 5. The cue is to check the mode (heard once, not reread) and the audience's age before choosing devices.

questions.stem: A student writes a hybrid crime story assembled from a police interview transcript, three text-message threads and a newspaper clipping, with no narrator. What does this structure most likely achieve?
options: The story no longer needs a narrative arc, because documents are not arranged in any sequence
Readers piece the events together from partial, competing sources, so gaps and bias become part of the meaning
Readers cannot form judgements about the characters at all, because no narrator is present to guide them
The story becomes factual rather than fictional, because transcripts and news reports are non-fiction forms
questions.explanation: A found-document or documentary hybrid withholds a single organising voice, so the reader does the assembling and the unreliability of each source is felt as part of the experience. The claim that readers cannot judge the characters is tempting but wrong: readers judge constantly, using tone, contradiction and what each document leaves out. Remember that removing a narrator shifts interpretive work onto the reader rather than shutting interpretation down.

questions.stem: A student is redrafting a story narrated by an exhausted night-shift nurse. The draft reads: 'I was very tired. The ward was busy. I did my job.' Which redraft best develops a distinctive voice for this narrator?
options: 'Fourteen hours in, the ward hummed like a fridge and I moved through it on autopilot, counting doors.'
'I was exhausted, drained, worn out and utterly shattered, and the ward was busy, hectic and frantic.'
'The nurse was extremely fatigued and the ward exceptionally busy, but she completed all her duties.'
'It was a busy night on the ward, as anyone in nursing will tell you, and tiredness comes with the job.'
questions.explanation: Voice comes from specific perception and rhythm: a precise detail ('fourteen hours in'), an odd but exact comparison and a small habitual action show us how this narrator experiences the ward rather than telling us she is tired. The version stacking synonyms is tempting because it sounds more expressive, but repeating near-identical adjectives adds intensity without adding any individual way of seeing. When redrafting for voice, look for concrete detail and characteristic rhythm, not for more adjectives.

questions.stem: A student's hybrid story about a missing bushwalker is built from search-party radio transcripts, a ranger's incident report and the walker's own trail notes. In feedback, what is the strongest reason to keep the trail notes in a loose, fragmentary style while keeping the report clipped and formal?
options: Fragmentary writing is always more literary than formal writing, so it should dominate the piece
Official documents must be reproduced word for word from real examples, so their style cannot be altered
The contrast in voice lets the reader feel the walker's disorientation against the official record's detachment
Varying the styles proves the student can write in more than one register, which is what hybrid texts are assessed on
questions.explanation: In a hybrid text the point of mixing forms is that each form carries its own voice, and the friction between those voices creates meaning for the reader. The option about proving range is tempting because variety is genuinely on display, but it justifies the choice by what it shows about the writer rather than by its effect on the reader. Strong feedback on experimentation always names the effect on the audience.

questions.stem: In much writing by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors, people are frequently represented as connected to family, community and Country. What does analysing this representation most usefully involve?
options: Examining the specific language and structural choices through which the text builds those connections
Assuming every Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander text carries the same message about identity
Treating the text as a factual information source about a culture rather than as literature
Judging the text by how closely its characters resemble those in non-Indigenous Australian novels
questions.explanation: Analysis always returns to how the text works: the imagery, narration, sequencing and word choice through which connection is built for a reader. Assuming a shared single message is a tempting shortcut, but it flattens the enormous diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations, histories and authors. The cue is that a question about representation is asking about craft in this particular text, not about generalisations across a group of authors.

questions.stem: A memoir by an Aboriginal author includes this moment: 'Nan showed me the waterhole her own mother had swum in, and named each bird as it came down to drink.' What is the strongest analysis of how people and place are represented here?
options: The description is purely factual reporting, so it does not shape the reader's view at all
Place is represented as holding family history and knowledge that is passed between generations
Place is represented as empty country that the narrator's family is only visiting for the day
The narrator is represented as cut off from family and reliant on her own observations
questions.explanation: Two details do the work: the waterhole is linked to an earlier generation, and the naming of birds shows knowledge being handed on, so people and place are represented as bound together across time. The claim that the passage is purely factual is the most tempting distractor, because the sentence is plain and unadorned — but the choice to mention the great-grandmother and the naming is exactly what shapes meaning. Plain language still carries selection, and selection is representation.

questions.stem: A nineteenth-century British novel describes an Australian valley as 'idle country, lying open and waiting for better hands'. What does this description most clearly show about the text's representation of place?
options: The description proves that no people were living in or caring for that valley
The land is represented through a colonial viewpoint that frames it as unused and available
The land is represented factually, since the narrator gives no opinion about the settlers
The phrase is a simile comparing the valley to a labourer resting between shifts
questions.explanation: Words like 'idle' and 'waiting' assign the land a lack and a purpose, framing it as unproductive until Europeans arrive — a value-laden colonial representation, not a neutral description. The claim that it proves nobody lived there is the dangerous distractor: a text's viewpoint tells us what the writer's culture assumed, never what was actually true of a place or its people. Look for evaluative words like 'idle' and 'better' as signals of viewpoint.

questions.stem: You are analysing an Australian translation of a Japanese novel set in a coastal village. What is the most important thing to take into account about its representation of that place?
options: The translation strips out cultural context, so the village should be read as though it were Australian
Because the language is not the author's own, only plot and character can be analysed reliably
Translated texts represent places less accurately than texts written in the reader's own language
The wording you are reading involves the translator's choices, so descriptions are mediated twice over
questions.explanation: A translated text reaches you through two sets of decisions — the author's and the translator's — so when you quote a phrase you are analysing a rendering, and it is worth acknowledging that. The claim that only plot and character can be analysed is tempting, but translated language can still be analysed closely, as long as you note that the wording is a translator's version. Signal this in your writing with phrases such as 'in this translation'.

questions.stem: In analysing representations of people, what is a stereotype?
options: A character whose behaviour stays consistent from beginning to end
A reduced, repeated set of traits assigned to a group, replacing complexity
Any character described with strong adjectives and physical detail
A minor character who appears briefly and is not fully developed
questions.explanation: A stereotype flattens a whole group into a few repeated traits, so the individual character carries the label rather than a personality. The option about a minor character is the closest trap: brief characters can be lightly sketched without being stereotyped, because sketchiness is about how much page space they get, not about recycling group assumptions. Ask whether the traits come from a group cliché or from that particular person's situation.

questions.stem: Two novels represent the same stretch of river country: one written by a settler author in 1890 calls it 'empty, silent land'; one written by an Aboriginal author in 2015 names its waterholes, seasons and the families who camp there. What is the most defensible analytical point about this pair?
options: The 1890 novel is a poor description of the place, while the 2015 novel is an objective description of how the place really is
The two novels cannot be compared because they were written in different centuries for different reading audiences
Each representation reflects the author's cultural position and purpose, so comparing them reveals what each text includes and leaves out
The 2015 novel is the more skilfully written text, since naming specific places is always better literary craft than general description
questions.explanation: Comparing representations of the same place shows how a writer's context and purpose shape selection: the word 'empty' erases the people already present, while naming waterholes and families asserts continuing connection. The 'objective description' option is the trap, because it treats one representation as neutral truth — but every text, including the 2015 novel, is constructed for a purpose. The clue is that comparison is about what each text does, not about ranking one as reality and the other as error.

questions.stem: 'At first I thought the mother was cruel; by chapter twelve I saw she was frightened.' This shows:
options: Identified the author's message about parenthood
Corrected a misreading caused by early inattention
Compared this mother with mothers in other novels
Tracked a change in their impression while reading
questions.explanation: The sentence names an initial impression and a later one, which is exactly what comparing impressions looks like. 'Corrected a misreading caused by not paying attention' is the most tempting distractor, but a shifting impression is a normal, valid effect of how texts release information gradually — it is not evidence of careless reading. Look for the 'at first... but later' pattern: it signals a developing response, not an error being fixed.

questions.stem: Which addition would most strengthen the response 'I did not like the narrator at first, but I ended up sympathising with him'?
options: Reference to the specific scenes and details that caused the shift in sympathy
A statement that most other readers in the class felt the same way about him
A summary of everything the narrator does over the course of the novel
A general claim that all narrators become more likeable as a novel goes on
questions.explanation: A developed personal response is anchored in evidence: naming the moments and details that produced the change turns a bare reaction into an argument about the text. Citing class agreement is tempting because it sounds like support, but popularity of a view is not textual evidence and does not explain the shift. Ask yourself 'what in the text did this?' — that question pushes a response from reaction to analysis.

questions.stem: After a class discussion, a student writes: 'I still think the father is selfish, but I now understand why others read his silence as grief.' What does this response best demonstrate?
options: A response developed by testing an initial impression against other readings without abandoning it
A failure to reach a conclusion, since the student has not chosen one reading over the other
A shift in impression, because the student has adopted the interpretation offered by classmates
Agreement that both readings are equally supported, so the text has no determinable meaning
questions.explanation: Developing a response includes holding a position while genuinely engaging with alternatives, which shows the reader has tested their impression rather than merely repeated it. 'A failure to reach a conclusion' is the tempting distractor, but the student does state a clear view — they simply also account for a rival reading, which strengthens rather than weakens the response. The cue is 'I still think': the position is stated, then defended in the light of other views.

questions.stem: While reading a novel, a student writes short journal entries after chapters 1, 10 and 20, recording what they think of the protagonist each time. What is the best use of these entries when writing a developed personal response?
options: Count how many times the opinion changed and use that number as the main point
Quote an early entry beside a later one and explain which scenes caused the view to change
Rewrite the earlier entries so that they match the final view and read consistently
Delete the earlier entries, since a first impression carries no analytical value
questions.explanation: A developed response uses the journal as evidence of a reading journey, anchoring each stage to the text that produced it. Rewriting earlier entries to match the final view destroys exactly the material the task needs — the contrast between then and now. Ask yourself: does this use of the journal show movement caused by the text, or does it flatten it?

questions.stem: A student's first impression of a poem is that it is a gentle description of a summer field. After learning the poet wrote it while serving in a war, the student rereads it and finds the same field imagery unsettling. What is the strongest way to handle this in a written response?
options: Explain how the context gave new weight to details already in the poem, quoting those details
Argue that the words of the poem changed meaning at the moment the context was learned
State that the first reading was simply a misreading and base the response on the second only
Base the response on the poet's war service, since context makes close reference to the poem unnecessary
questions.explanation: Context does not alter the words on the page; it changes what a reader notices and how much weight they give it, so the shift must be traced back through specific images and phrasing. The claim that the poem's meaning changed the moment the context was learned locates the change in the text rather than in the reader, which is not what happened. The reliable cue: a subsequent impression is still an argument about the text, so it must be evidenced from the text.

questions.stem: A teacher asks students to write one sentence that compares their initial and subsequent impressions of a novel. Which sentence actually does this?
options: "Ruby is a bully in the early chapters, and she visits her mother in hospital in chapter nine before returning to school."
"By the end of the novel I had decided that Ruby is one of the most convincing characters I have read this year."
"Ruby is a much harsher character than the older sister in the short story we studied last term, who is gentle throughout."
"Reading the first chapter I dismissed Ruby as a bully, but after her hospital visit in chapter nine I read her sharpness as fear."
questions.explanation: Comparing initial and subsequent impressions means naming what you first thought, naming what you thought later, and pointing to the part of the text that shifted you — which is exactly what the sentence about dismissing Ruby then rereading her sharpness as fear does. The sentence that summarises her bullying and the hospital visit is tempting because it mentions the same two moments, but it only retells events and records no impression at all. The sentence about deciding by the end gives a single final judgement with nothing to compare it to, and the sentence about the older sister compares two texts rather than two stages of one reader's response. Cue: look for two time markers about your own reading, such as "at first" and "after", not two plot points.

questions.stem: What is a stanza?
options: The rhythm a poem follows
The rhyme at a line's end
A group of lines in a poem
A single line of a poem
questions.explanation: Stanzas are to poems what paragraphs are to prose — a block of lines set off by a space. Verse is often used loosely for the same thing, but a stanza is the structural unit you can point at on the page.
questions.teaching:
Poetry is laid out in units the way prose is, and the vocabulary for those units is worth having straight.

The building block is the line, which in poetry ends where the poet decides rather than where the page runs out. Lines are grouped into blocks separated by white space, and those blocks work rather like paragraphs — each usually developing one image or turn of thought. Some have fixed lengths with names of their own: a couplet is two, a quatrain four. Rhythm and rhyme scheme are separate features again, describing sound rather than layout on the page.

questions.stem: What is the setting of a story?
options: Where and when the story takes place
The problem the main character faces
The order the events are told in
The message the writer wants to send
questions.explanation: Setting covers both place and period, and it does more work than it looks: a story set in a drought or a lockdown gets much of its pressure from that alone. The problem the character faces is the conflict, which is the tempting near-miss.
questions.teaching:
Narratives are usually analysed through a small set of elements, and questions test whether you can tell them apart.

One element is the situation the story is placed in — both the location and the period, which together shape what is possible and what is at stake. Another is the problem driving the story forward. A third is the sequence of events. A fourth is the underlying idea the story explores. The first of these does more than provide scenery: a story placed in a drought, a war or a lockdown draws much of its pressure from that alone.

questions.stem: What is a theme?
options: The place where the story is set
A character who appears throughout
An idea about life the whole text explores
The sequence of events in the plot
questions.explanation: A theme is what a text is *about* underneath what happens — loyalty, guilt, belonging. Retelling the plot is the usual substitute, but plot is the events and theme is the idea running under them.
questions.teaching:
There is a useful distinction between what happens in a text and what the text is about.

What happens is the plot — the sequence of events you could summarise for someone. What it is about sits underneath: an idea concerning human experience that the whole text keeps returning to, such as belonging, betrayal, forgiveness or the cost of ambition. It is usually implied rather than stated, which is why two readers can identify different ones in the same book and both be defensible. Retelling the plot is the standard substitute in essays, and it is what loses marks.

questions.stem: What is a rhetorical question?
options: A question asked for effect, not for an answer
A question a character asks another character
A question the reader is expected to research
A question that opens every paragraph
questions.explanation: 'How much longer can we wait?' is not seeking information — it is pushing the audience towards a conclusion they supply themselves. That is why it turns up constantly in speeches and editorials.
questions.teaching:
Persuasive writers use several devices that involve questions, and this one is a question in form only.

The speaker is not seeking information and does not pause for a reply. Instead the question is framed so the audience supplies the intended answer themselves — 'how much longer can we wait?' pushes towards a conclusion far more effectively than stating it would. Because the listener does the concluding, they feel they arrived at it independently, which is precisely why speeches and editorials are full of them.

questions.stem: What is an antagonist?
options: The character telling the story
The main character of the story
A character who appears only briefly
The force working against the main character
questions.explanation: The antagonist opposes the protagonist, and it need not be a villain or even a person — a storm, an illness or a legal system can do the job. Confusing it with the protagonist is the standard slip.
questions.teaching:
Character roles are defined by their function in the story rather than by their personality.

The character whose goal drives the narrative is the protagonist. Whatever stands in the way of that goal fills the opposing role — and it need not be a villain, or even a person. A rival, a parent, an illness, a bureaucracy, a storm, or the character's own fear can all fill it. Some stories have the same character in both roles. The useful question is not 'who is bad?' but 'what is preventing the main character from getting what they want?'

questions.stem: What is repetition used for in a text?
options: To separate one paragraph from another
To emphasise an idea and make it memorable
To fill space when a writer runs short
To show the writer is uncertain
questions.explanation: Deliberate repetition drives an idea home and gives a passage rhythm — think of any speech you can still quote. Accidental repetition is a different thing, and the difference is whether it earns its place.
questions.teaching:
Repetition appears in writing for two very different reasons, and telling them apart is the skill being tested.

Accidental repetition — the same word four times in a paragraph because nothing better came to mind — weakens writing. Deliberate repetition does the opposite: it drives an idea home, builds rhythm, and makes a phrase stick. Think of any speech you can still quote from memory and you will find a repeated structure at its centre. Related devices have their own names: anaphora repeats the opening of successive clauses, and a refrain repeats a whole line.

questions.stem: What is an anecdote in persuasive writing?
options: A short personal story used to make a point
A statistic quoted from a study
A quotation from a recognised expert
A definition given at the start
questions.explanation: An anecdote makes an abstract argument concrete and invites the reader to feel it rather than weigh it. That is its strength and its weakness: one story is vivid but proves very little on its own.
questions.teaching:
Persuasive texts use several kinds of support, and each works on the reader differently.

Statistics and expert opinion appeal to reason and carry weight through authority. A short personal story works a different way: it makes an abstract argument concrete and invites the reader to feel it rather than weigh it. That vividness is its power, and also its weakness — a single case proves very little about the general pattern, which is exactly why writers reach for one when the general pattern is not on their side. Good analysis names both the effect and the limitation.

questions.stem: What is the narrative point of view?
options: The order the events are arranged in
The place the story is set in
Who is telling the story and how much they know
The moral the story is teaching
questions.explanation: Point of view decides what you are allowed to see. A narrator inside the story can only report what they know, which is what makes an unreliable narrator possible at all.
questions.teaching:
How a story is told shapes what a reader is allowed to know, and that is what this term captures.

A narrator inside the events refers to themselves and can only report what they personally know, saw or were told — which means they can be mistaken, biased, or lying, and the unreliable narrator exists entirely because of that limit. A narrator outside the events may know only one character's thoughts, or everyone's. Deciding what a narrator can and cannot see is often the most revealing thing you can say about a text's construction.
